# Microorganisms (living things too small to see) (`microorganisms`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/biology.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Life sciences (`biology`)
- Deps: needs microscope; helped by clear_glass, heat_sterilisation
- Core idea: A drop of pond water, rain water that has stood for some days, or the white scraping from between the teeth swarms with living creatures far too small for the eye, of many shapes, moving and multiplying. They are seen with a single tiny lens of very short focus (a glass bead about 1–2 mm across, set in a hole in a metal plate and held close to the eye with the sample lit from behind), which can magnify the sample about 200 times. Living pond organisms differ in shape and movement. Bacteria are smaller still; the quality of the lens and the lighting matter as much as nominal magnification. In later laboratory work, separate colonies helped distinguish organisms in mixed samples. A colony may start from a clump of cells, so its appearance alone cannot establish purity or identify the organism.
- Pitfalls:
  - Trying with spectacle lenses or an early two-lens microscope; until about 1830 the simple bead lens showed far more
  - Concluding that because they exist they cause disease; nobody made that case convincingly for 200 years
  - Believing all of them are harmful; most are harmless and many are needed (bread, beer, cheese, soil)
  - Assuming they arise from the rotting matter in which they are found
- History: europe: 1658 – Kircher claims 'little worms' in plague blood (his microscope could not show bacteria); 1665 Hooke draws a microscopic mould; 1674–1676 Leeuwenhoek (Delft) sees protozoa and bacteria; 1683 bacteria from teeth; 1786 O. F. Müller classifies them; 1881 Koch's solid culture media; agar suggested by Fanny Hesse; 1884 Gram's stain; 1887 Petri's dish
- Read:
  - Clifford Dobell, Antony van Leeuwenhoek and His 'Little Animals' (1932)
  - Nick Lane, The unseen world: reflections on Leeuwenhoek (1677) 'Concerning little animals', Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2015)
